purpose: Durable owner-comment capture with anchors and full paragraph context. Source Word documents remain untouched; IDs are document-local. One private transport-origin postcode is redacted in this repository copy.

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Discovery before drafting. Ask competing questions of the material. Research should be allowed to change the proposed story, not merely furnish citations for it.
comments.comment: The researcher should also be allowed to "dig deeper" to supplement, explore, and enrich findings - either on their own (within guardrails to not disappear in unwarranted rabbit holes) or prompted by writer or orchestrator

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: The experience between stops. Approaches, transitions, contrasts, quiet and the end of the walk deserve editorial attention alongside the individual scripts.
comments.comment: Stories while walking are a big part of what I want here. It can give us more room to expand into broader, more thoughtful stories about the area, with a bit more freedom in subject, writing, and timing, as long as we find a way to connect it once or twice to what the user can see around them.

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: The Moth's advice makes desire, dilemma and consequences central to its true first-person stories. That is useful when a historical episode contains documented human stakes; its performance rules are not a universal definition of storytelling. [2] RaMell Ross describes Hale County This Morning, This Evening as an experience of a place, with meaning emerging through attention and the relationship between moments. That offers a different possibility. His method grew from sustained life within the community; a desk-researched tour cannot claim the same intimacy. [3]
comments.comment: We're going to be very upfront that this is AI generated and that comes with upsides and downsides.True. What we gain in trust in the veracity, we have to accept that we lose in human connection. We can intuit how people in the past felt, and recount e.g. reviews and personal accounts, and we can nudge the user into feeling a certain way, but we can't express e.g. personal preference.

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Your survey-first rule is a strong starting point. Existing tours reveal what knowledgeable guides have found worthwhile and how they connect it. They also reflect what is already easy to market and document. After the survey, look deliberately at ordinary local life, overlooked relationships and the questions that published routes leave unanswered. The catalogue should widen our options before we choose.
comments.comment: Not just tours but guides. These can build a large database of candidates, which we will annotate with some dimensions as we go - e.g. popular must-see, beyond the beaten path, music, true crime, whatever. This is just for future thinking, but existing tours are one of the obvious initial sources for the survey, and I'd like your help to think of a disciplined search programme that doesn't go completely nuts in volume but covers the bases before more googling happens. We need to think of both hyper-touristic places (central london) and less well documented ones

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Stopping rule: continue research while a plausible next source could change the central explanation, selection or scene. Once the account is supported and the remaining unknowns can be omitted or stated honestly, draft it. A narrow unknown about an incidental detail need not turn a pleasant tour into a research project without end.
comments.comment: This will require attentive formulation and testing to get it right but this is the correct direction

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: A useful draft asks what the listener knows at the start and what becomes clearer by the end. The change can be small: noticing an agreement in the shape of a garden, understanding why a local venue mattered, or recognising a vanished social world. The narrator need not announce this change as a moral.
comments.comment: As we move forward, I think we should probably develop an overarching editorial perspective, e.g. there is magic in the everyday life, or local communities have power, or beauty is everywhere - none of these are right, but as we move towards there, we could maybe build a set of values that can be shared through stories and tours. The AI is impartial, but this is my app and I feel like it should reflect my views to an extent

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
comments.anchor: finding the genuinely compelling part of the material
context: Ira Glass describes a productive relationship between events and reflection in his kind of radio storytelling. He also stresses finding the genuinely compelling part of the material and recognises exceptions to his usual narrative form. I would borrow that movement between the particular and its meaning, while avoiding a compulsory “big idea” at every stop. [4]
comments.comment: Are you clear on methods to do that? They can be intuitive - I expect the orchestrator agent to operate at a decent level of thinking - but as long as we could clearly explain it to a human editor I'd be ok. If not, let's do a bit more research on it and agree on a first draft of it

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Your Tally Ho feedback calls for the important road context before the secondary naming anecdote. That should guide this example. More generally, context needs to arrive before its absence causes confusion. It need not become a compulsory opening paragraph containing the whole chronology.
comments.comment: Just like the physical act of taking a walking tours, it's about grounding and a feeling of the user knowing where they are in the story. Lack of context can feel unmoored, or disjointed, and that's what we want to avoid

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
comments.anchor: through their role in this story
context: Introduce an unfamiliar person through their role in this story. Give a date where it locates a change or scene. Use a name again only when the listener needs to remember it. The aim is to make the account understandable on one hearing, not to remove every proper noun or interesting complication.
comments.comment: Or just a general statement, like you would do when writing a magazine article or a book - you don't just throw a name out there and move on, you make an effort to contextualise it. It can be 5 words or a full sentence, but it needs to happen

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
comments.anchor: stay consistent with what we know
context: Choose a period and a particular kind of activity. Establish the documented physical setting and the relevant social context. Then use plausible movement, sound and ordinary activity to make that setting imaginable, with a natural frame such as “Picture an evening here in…”. Individual sensory details need not each have an eyewitness record. The reconstruction should stay consistent with what we know.
comments.comment: Exactly. We can gauge confidence levels as well about these and keep / adjust them above a certain threshold

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: At Torrington, the performers' identities could determine what sort of scene is plausible. It would still take more evidence to describe the actual audience's clothes, reactions or a particular exchange on stage. Generic period knowledge can inform an imagined crowd without becoming a witnessed account of that advertised night.
comments.comment: Omg they're still alive and re-united! lots about their audience and cult following. Like for the Kinks bit, there's great value in these bits linking the past to the present, particularly in uncovering rare bits of knowledge in unlikely places; as long as we can contextualise them. Fair to assume the user might have heard of The Kinks (I guess?) but less likely for these two, even if they apparently have a serious cult following

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: An insight can say more than the source explicitly says. It should show its reasoning and remain proportionate to the evidence. “This suggests…” can introduce interpretation, but does not excuse a leap.
comments.comment: Even that feels clunky. We're not writing a freshman university essay - we need to tell a story with confidence, verve, and grace

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
comments.anchor: 25% ceiling is still untested and unapproved
context: Your digression cap should remain a time allowance. Before assigning one, distinguish context needed to understand this place from an excursion into a wider subject. Then ask what the excursion gives back to the local account. A short generic sermon can be worse than a longer, tightly connected explanation. The proposed 25% ceiling is still untested and unapproved; I would use a deliberate seconds allowance for the next draft, with the return to the place written into the outline.
comments.comment: yes agreed - it might take a more qualitative shape down the road if that's what works best

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: We have been evaluating the benefit of being at each stop. I would add the benefit of having travelled between them: a change of scale, noise, frontage or use can make the next story intelligible. Two individually modest places can make a strong pair; two excellent standalone accounts can still feel repetitive together.
comments.comment: But also travelling! Let's not lose sight of building stories for between stops. This can give us a lot more flexibility in tour design when we want a certain set but there are a few big gaps. Also will be 100% essential when we come full circle to car tours (as shaka guide was the original inspiration)

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Film provides useful craft analogies. An establishing view locates a scene. A close detail directs attention. Juxtaposition makes differences legible. Returning to an earlier image can give an ending its force. These are proposals for tour design, not proof that a walker responds like a cinema audience.
comments.comment: I like where this is going

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: A film controls its frame and timing; our visitor chooses where to look, may miss a cue and can encounter a changed street. Spoken orientation should invite and support attention without pretending to control the view. Never make a central explanation depend on spotting a tiny, unverified feature at an exact second.
comments.comment:
tiny feature: make sure to give good enough guidance and allow them time to find it. 
Unverified: the more I think about it the more I feel like an agent looking at streetview snapshots or something like that could be key. We'll have to think about the mechanisms and cost management

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Janet Cardiff and George Bures Miller's own description of their walks illustrates how recorded material and present surroundings can interact. Their work deliberately uses fiction and perceptual ambiguity; our historical narrator and directions need a different contract. We can learn from the importance of being there without importing simulated events or promising immersion from narration alone. [7]
comments.comment: Do they? Why? Not saying you're wrong but let's align on that

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: A topic might be entertainment; a more productive question is what kinds of gathering a neighbourhood made possible, for whom, and what survives. Different stops could supply pleasure, access, aspiration, exclusion or reinvention. They need not all confirm one answer.
comments.comment: I'm personally invested in the idea of something feeling insightful - which in my qual research career I've always linked to the question "why"

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
comments.anchor: theme should be proposed after the survey
context: A theme should be proposed after the survey, challenged by research, and revised before final writing. A memorable outlier may earn a place as relief or contrast. If it requires a strained bridge, admit that it is a delightful aside or omit it.
comments.comment: What I am thinking, which might be over-engineering, is that we could aim to end the survey with significantly enough candidates to enable curation to happens in a combination of routing and thematic coherence

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: A theme should be proposed after the survey, challenged by research, and revised before final writing. A memorable outlier may earn a place as relief or contrast. If it requires a strained bridge, admit that it is a delightful aside or omit it.
comments.comment: With all that being said, yes a theme can absolutely be loosely retrofitted. I don't intend "themed tours" to be the be all and end all. Discovery and oddities has its own charm, and I think that's what 90% of self-guided walking tour books do.

comments.author: Sidi Lemine

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: The houses stand back from the road, behind a strip of greenery. When the villas were laid out from 1867, that open space was part of the deal. Their hundred-year leases required it to stay unbuilt and planted. So the layout included a restriction on what could fill the gap. The buildings tell you where construction happened; the garden helps you picture a limit placed on it. The surviving historical account does not tell us who maintains the ground today, so it would be a mistake to call it a residents' cooperative.
comments.comment: see I would connect these sentences: "to stay unbuilt and planted, so the layout included"

comments.author: Sidi Lemine

context: Picture choosing a home here in the years after 1867. There is the house, of course: its own front door, its windows facing the road. comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: Picture reading this bill in June 1977. Eighty pence, Sunday evening, John Otway and Wild Willy Barrett. Their later account describes a partnership built on contrasts: Barrett's musical skill and dry humour alongside Otway's unruly showmanship. By December, the pair would be in the singles chart with Really Free. That future was still ahead of this little advert. The attraction here is the possibility of encountering an act locally before knowing what would become of it.

comments.author: Sidi Lemine
context: 99% Invisible, “Curb Cuts”. My craft takeaway is the connection between a concrete thing and a wider mechanism. We should not transplant Berkeley's history onto a London pavement or require its long podcast structure at one stop. This is a transcript study, not a new listening assessment. [8]
comments.comment: I LOVE 99PI. the writing, the research, the narration - I would be very happy to emulate them in that regard
